steps.body: Time for official names. The bottom number is the **denominator** — it names the KIND of piece (the cut). The top is the **numerator** — it's the NUMBER of pieces (the count). Memory hook: numerator ≈ 'number of'; denominator ≈ 'what denomination' — like coin kinds.

widget.prompt: Whose job is it — the numerator (top) or the denominator (bottom)?

items.label: Counts how many pieces you take
items.feedback: Counting is the top's whole career.

items.label: Tells how the whole was cut
Sets the SIZE of each piece
items.feedback: Piece size comes straight from the cut — finer cut, smaller pieces. Bottom's job.

items.label: Grows by one each time you grab another piece
items.feedback: Another piece, another tick of the count — the top climbs.

widget.missFeedback: Ask: is this about CUTTING (bottom) or COUNTING (top)?
widget.successFeedback: Cutting and sizing belong to the denominator; counting and climbing belong to the numerator.

predict.prompt: If the BOTTOM number grows while the top stays put, does your amount grow or shrink?
predict.reveal: A bigger bottom means the whole was cut into more, smaller pieces — holding the same count of tinier pieces is holding less.

explanationVariants: The 9 sits on the bottom, so it's the denominator — the whole was cut into ninths.
Bottom = kind of piece. The 9 says these are ninth-pieces.

options.label: Denominator — the whole was cut into 9 pieces
Numerator — it counts the pieces taken
options.feedback: The counter is the TOP number — here, the 4. The 9 below records the cut.

options.label: The answer to the fraction
options.feedback: A fraction isn't a problem waiting for an answer — it's a description: 4 pieces of a 9-cut.

options.label: A remainder
options.feedback: Remainders belong to division-with-leftovers. In a fraction, the 9 is the cut count — the denominator.

steps.body: Watch each dial work alone. **Fix the bottom, raise the top:** 1/6 → 2/6 → 3/6 — more pieces, more of the whole. **Fix the top, raise the bottom:** 1/2 → 1/4 → 1/8 — same count, but each piece shrinks, so you hold LESS. Two dials, opposite feels.

explanationVariants: Raising the denominator cuts the whole into more, smaller pieces — one piece of a 9-cut is a sliver next to one of a 3-cut.
Same top (one piece), finer cut: your single piece shrinks. The bottom dial works in reverse of what big numbers usually mean.

widget.prompt: Keep the top at 1 and turn the bottom dial up: 1/3 becomes 1/9. Your amount of the whole…

options.label: Shrinks — the cut got finer
options.feedback: Nine-way cutting makes small pieces; your single piece is now a sliver.

options.label: Grows — 9 is bigger than 3
options.feedback: The big-number reflex! On the bottom, a bigger number means MORE cuts — and more cuts make each piece smaller, not bigger.

options.label: Stays the same
options.feedback: The count stayed at one, but the piece KIND changed — a ninth is far smaller than a third.

options.label: Becomes zero
options.feedback: You still hold a real piece — just a small one. 1/9 is little, not nothing.

widget.prompt: Why can't the denominator be 0? Step through it.

panels.title: The bottom is a cut count
panels.body: Cut a bar into 3 pieces — fine. Into 2 — fine. Now try cutting it into ZERO pieces…

panels.title: Zero pieces means no bar
panels.body: A cut into zero pieces would make the whole bar vanish. There's no piece to pick up, so '1/0' describes nothing at all.

panels.title: Zero upstairs is fine
panels.body: 0/4 just means 'cut into fourths, take none' — an empty hand, perfectly legal. Zero on TOP is allowed; zero on the BOTTOM is forbidden.

widget.continueFeedback: Keep stepping — the forbidden number shows itself in the next panel.
widget.successFeedback: The cut must make at least one piece — so the denominator is never 0, while the numerator happily can be.

explanationVariants: Cut count downstairs (8), take count on top (3): 3/8.
Denominator records the cut, numerator the take — the recipe maps straight onto the two floors.

commonEntries.feedback: Jobs swapped — 8/3 reads 'cut into 3, take 8': more than two whole bars!
Right cut, wrong count — 5/8 takes five pieces; this recipe takes three.
Right count, wrong cut — the bar was cut into 8, so the denominator must say 8.

widget.fallbackFeedback: The cut count (8) goes on the bottom; the take count (3) on top.
widget.successFeedback: Take 3 on top, cut of 8 below — the recipe written as a fraction.

hints: Read Sam's story again: what was the cut, and what was the take?
The cut count belongs on the bottom.
The cut here is 6; the take is 2.
explanationVariants: The cut (6) belongs downstairs and the take (2) on top: 2/6. Sam's 6/2 reads as 'cut into 2, take 6' — three whole cakes.
Denominator = cut = 6; numerator = take = 2. Swapping the jobs turns a small share into a bakery order.

widget.prompt: Sam cuts a cake into 6 equal pieces and takes 2 — then writes 6/2. Write what it SHOULD say.

commonEntries.feedback: Test it as a recipe: 6/2 says 'cut into 2, take 6 pieces' — six halves is three cakes, not two small pieces of one.
6/6 takes ALL six pieces — the whole cake. Sam only took two.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Read the story again: the cut goes on the bottom (denominator), the take on top (numerator).
widget.successFeedback: The cut (6) goes downstairs, the take (2) on top. 6/2 would be six pieces of a HALF-cut — three whole cakes!

takeaways: Denominator (bottom) = the cut — it names the piece kind and sets piece size.
Numerator (top) = the count — how many pieces you take.
Zero can sit on top (take nothing) but never on the bottom (a cut must make pieces).
steps.teaser: next chapter: fractions leave the pizza and move onto the number line.

concept.body: Quick rewind. Memory hook: **D for Down and for Denominator** — the cut lives downstairs. Whatever's left rides on top: the numerator, your piece count.

explanationVariants: The piece KIND comes from the cut — the downstairs 7 says these are sevenths.
D for Down: the denominator 7 names the pieces; the 2 upstairs just counts them.

widget.prompt: In 2/7, which number tells you the KIND of piece?

options.label: The 7 — the pieces are sevenths
options.feedback: Downstairs number, cut record, piece kind: sevenths.

options.label: The 2 — the pieces are halves
options.feedback: The 2 only COUNTS pieces. Their kind comes from the cut downstairs: sevenths.

options.label: Both together
options.feedback: Each has one job: the 7 names the kind (sevenths); the 2 counts them. Kind is the 7's alone.
